text.p: Renault chairman Louis Schweitzer reiterated on Thursday the carmaker's objective to break even this year.
The company had "the objective to return to equilibrium from this year", he told a news conference.
He also said that the controversial planned closure of the Vilvoorde plant in Belgium was tough but necessary.
Schweitzer also reiterated that the group believed it had rigorously respected Belgian law as regards notification of the plant closure.

He said Renault management at Vilvoorde had warned workers of the risks facing the plant more than two months ago and that he had gone personally to see Belgian Prime Minister Jean-Luc Dehaene in Brussels on February 21.
The closure was announced on February 27.
He said he hoped the Belgian plant would resume activities as soon as possible and that a dialogue concerning the closure would also begin.
"If one thing is untrue it's that on Renault's or my part there's a refusal for a dialogue," he said.

He said the workers at the Vilvoorde plant were of high quality. There were reasons to believe that a good number might be re-deployed elsewhere in the group and others might receive early retirement packages.
The plant employs 3,100 people. Schweitzer said that the wages at the Belgian plant were 25-30 percent higher than those in France and even higher than those in Spain.
He said wage costs were only one factor in the closure which was driven mainly by industrial logic as part of a reorganisation of Renault's European car assembly operations.
The company also said this week it would cut 2,764 jobs in France, but Schweitzer said no further job reductions were planned. The group had previously cut jobs in Spain.
"There are no further job reductions expected in Renault's European system," he said.

Asked about European Competition Commissioner Karl van Miert's decision to block Spanish government subsidies for Renault's Valladolid plant, Schweitzer said there was no linkage between the investments at Valladolid and the closure at Vilvoorde.
He said he was not sure it was a good idea to hold one project hostage for an unrelated matter.
Schweitzer added that there were no talks under way at the moment with potential buyers for the Vilvoorde plant.
"If a competitor is interested we would facilitate the process," he said.
